External Angle Bisector

GeometryTrianglesAlgebra
Game: Drag the corners of a triangle to see the line that splits the angle outside A and where it meets the far side.
How to play: Drag A, B or C with a mouse or finger, or focus a corner and use the arrow keys. Turn on Hint or Extra construction, then press Check the ratio.
Look for the math

The bisector of the angle inside a triangle cuts the far side in a special ratio. Surprisingly, the bisector of the angle outside that corner cuts the extended far side in the very same ratio. Drag the corners and compare the two numbers under the picture.

The inside and outside bisectors

An angle bisector splits an angle into two equal parts. The outside bisector at A is at right angles to the inside one: the two arcs at A show its equal halves. It meets the line BC at D, which normally lies outside the segment BC — unless AB and AC are equal, when the two lines are parallel and there is no meeting point. The page claims that for the inside foot, and again for this outside foot,

AB / AC = DB / DC

This is the Angle Bisector Theorem. The logic test checks it on a grid of shapes and on hundreds of random triangles, in both drawing orders, and it holds every time.

The parallel through C

Draw the line through C parallel to AD and let it meet the line AB at E; turning on Extra construction shows it. Since CE is parallel to AD, the angle at E equals the acute angle the outside bisector makes with AB, and the angle at C equals the half angle 90° − BAC/2. So triangle AEC is isosceles and AE = AC. The similar triangles BEC and BAD then give BE / BA = BC / BD = CE / AD, which rearranges to the ratio above.

A typo in the original angle lines

The original page prints angle AEC = angle BAD = 90° − BAC/2 and then angle ACE = 180° − angle CAE − angle AEC = 90° = BAC/2. Checked against the picture, the last equality is wrong: the true result is angle ACE = angle AEC = 90° − BAC/2. In a right triangle at A both are 45°, while the page would require 90° = 45°. The first line is the acute angle between the line AD and AB; which end of that line D lies on decides whether the angle at A itself is 90° − BAC/2 or its supplement. The logic test asserts the corrected identity and the failure of the printed one.

Where three bisectors meet

Write the three ratios at A, B and C and multiply them: the pieces cancel, which is the statement of Ceva's theorem. One inside bisector and the two outside bisectors at the other corners therefore meet at one point, the excenter opposite A. The test checks this on the same grid of triangles.

Try making AB much longer than AC, then turn on Hint to watch the parallel steps carry the ratio across the sides.
